card_roles.Arcane Signet: Two mana, a usable colour, every single time. Unglamorous — and never a dead draw.
card_roles.Ashnod's Altar: A free outlet that turns bodies into {C}{C}, which is real acceleration in a deck making free tokens. Know both halves: its famous Mikaeus pairing is refuted; its Skullclamp pairing is a combo-graph entry and does what it says.
card_roles.Bastion of Remembrance: Table-wide drain in enchantment form — a wrath can't touch it, and it brings its own body. One of three cards the build plan classifies as a dedicated wincon.
card_roles.Birds of Paradise: A one-drop that fixes both colours and, being a creature, doubles as fodder, a blocker and a Skullclamp target.
card_roles.Bitterblossom: A free body every upkeep for 1 life. Faerie Rogues are Skullclamp fodder, sacrifice fodder and chump blockers, and it rebuilds through wraths on its own.
card_roles.Black Sun's Zenith: Not a reset button — a rebuild. X counters on *each* creature triggers Hapatra once per creature, feeds Nest of Scarabs, and hands Necroskitter every opposing creature that dies with a counter on it.
card_roles.Blasting Station: An outlet that's also a converter — it untaps whenever a creature enters, so a token stream becomes repeatable damage with no drain payoff needed. Refuted as a Mikaeus two-card infinite.
card_roles.Blood Artist: Drains one *target player* per death, not each opponent — a value card and a wrath-tax, never your table clock. Verified in stack 001 converting the Druid loop at one life per cycle.
card_roles.Blowfly Infestation: The headline two-card kill on paper — 16.3% assembled per goldfish — and unverified. Play it for what it reliably is: a mandatory counter placement every time any creature dies with a counter on it, a genuine repeating source for Hapatra in ordinary games.
card_roles.Carrion Feeder: A free outlet — and actively anti-synergistic with Mikaeus, because it puts +1/+1 counters on itself, precisely what undying will not tolerate. Refuted as a Mikaeus infinite.
card_roles.Chrome Mox: Free acceleration that eats a coloured card from your hand. A Game Changer, and the exiled card is a real cost in a deck this dense with singleton answers.
card_roles.Contagion Clasp: A counter on entry, then repeatable proliferate. Slow — but it's a permanent source in a deck short on repeatable sources.
card_roles.Crumbling Ashes: Destroys a creature with a -1/-1 counter at each of your upkeeps. In a deck that sprays counters, that's repeating unconditional removal.
card_roles.Dark Ritual: Three black off one — your classic route to a turn-1 Hapatra or an ahead-of-curve Yawgmoth.
card_roles.Deadly Dispute: Two cards plus a Treasure, at instant speed, for a body you were losing anyway. Classified as draw, not ramp — the Treasure is a rider.
card_roles.Demonic Tutor: The cleanest tutor in the format and a Game Changer. Fetch a repeatable counter source first, a table-wide converter second.
card_roles.Devoted Druid: Half of your one verified two-card infinite. Its untap pays a -1/-1 counter as a cost — a free repeatable source in disguise — and under Mikaeus it resets itself forever: for deaths and Snakes, not mana.
card_roles.Diabolic Intent: Any card to hand with a body as the additional cost — nearly free here, because the body was fodder and its death is a trigger.
card_roles.Elvish Mystic: The fourth copy of the same effect. When your commander costs two and lands on turn 2 in 99.9% of runs, this is what makes turn 1 possible.
card_roles.Eternal Witness: Rebuys the tutor, sweeper or combo piece that got answered — on a body that's itself sacrifice fodder.
card_roles.Fixing lands: Bayou, Command Tower, City of Brass, Mana Confluence, Exotic Orchard, Spire of Industry, Conduit Pylons, Gond Gate, Hidden Grotto, Darkbore Pathway, Wastewood Verge, The Grey Havens, Tarnished Citadel, Forbidden Orchard and Gemstone Caverns fill out a 24-land base with zero lands entering tapped, 23 sources of each colour against a target of 22, and 91.8% on-curve for both pips off lands alone. One trap: Forbidden Orchard gives an opponent a Spirit each time you tap it — and that Spirit is a legal target for your own -1/-1 counters.
card_roles.Flourishing Defenses: A third mint on the same trigger — an Elf Warrior on every -1/-1 placement. Your only five-drop, and a combo-graph Blowfly partner whose loop is unresolved.
card_roles.Fume Spitter: A one-mana, free, instant-speed -1/-1 source: a Snake, a dead X/1 and a body for a sacrifice cost, all for one card.
card_roles.Green Sun's Zenith: A green creature straight onto the battlefield — Devoted Druid or Ivy Lane Denizen with the tempo attached, not just a card in hand.
card_roles.Grim Affliction: Instant-speed counter placement plus proliferate: a Snake at flash speed, or a second counter on something already shrinking.
card_roles.Grim Haruspex: Draws on every nontoken creature you control dying — the card that makes your sacrifice half free instead of costly. Morph gives it a floor when you need a body more than a trigger.
card_roles.Grim Monolith: Three colourless with a {4} untap. A Game Changer — but neither Vault nor Monolith makes coloured mana, and your costs are pip-heavy.
card_roles.Grim Tutor: Any card to hand for three mana and 3 life. Not a Game Changer, and the price is real in a deck that pays life everywhere else.
card_roles.Hapatra, Vizier of Poisons: The mint. Her second ability converts any -1/-1 counter placement into a 1/1 deathtouch Snake, once per event rather than per counter; her combat trigger is a bonus on an unevasive 2/2 and never a plan (verified stack 001, step 11).
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: Hexproof and indestructible for your whole board at instant speed — the one card that beats a targeted answer to your combo piece and a wrath at the same time.
card_roles.Host of the Hereafter: Moves counters from a dying creature onto another creature you control. Its only combo-graph partner in the entire graph is Hapatra — and whether *moving* counters counts as *putting* them is exactly the unresolved question.
card_roles.Imperial Seal: Sorcery-speed Vampiric Tutor. A Game Changer — slow enough that you want it early rather than at the pivot.
card_roles.Ivy Lane Denizen: A +1/+1 counter on target creature whenever another green creature you control enters. Six of the listed infinites pair it with outlets that make nothing enter — read those six as projection artifacts, unverified either way.
card_roles.Lightning Greaves: Protection and haste at {0} equip — and the specific card that restores mana to the Devoted Druid loop, netting four green per cycle as a main-phase-only three-card line. The trap: shroud locks Hapatra and Yawgmoth out of targeting the wearer.
card_roles.Llanowar Elves: Turn-1 acceleration into a turn-2 Hapatra, and a body you can eat later.
card_roles.Lotus Petal: One free mana of any colour, once — what turns an explosive keep from aspirational to functional.
card_roles.Mana Vault: Three mana off a one-drop, with an untap tax and upkeep damage. A Game Changer and pure speed — spend it on a turn that matters.
card_roles.Mikaeus, the Unhallowed: The combo hinge and a trap in one card. Undying on every other non-Human creature powers the two verified lines, while the same +1/+1 anthem keeps a counterless Walking Ballista alive at 1/1 and may switch off your own token loops — an open question flagged in the stack notes.
card_roles.Morbid Opportunist: Once-per-turn card advantage off any creature dying, yours or theirs. Cheap insurance that turns a sweeper into a card.
card_roles.Mox Diamond: Free acceleration that eats a land. A Game Changer — and it makes any colour, which is what separates it from the colourless rocks.
card_roles.Necroskitter: Turns their shrunken board into yours — any creature an opponent controls that dies with a -1/-1 counter on it comes back under your control. It is verified *absent* from the combo graph, so treat the Black Sun's Zenith pairing as strong oracle reasoning, not a confirmed line.
card_roles.Nest of Scarabs: A parallel mint that reads *that many* Insects, so it scales with counter volume in a way Hapatra doesn't. Its in-deck Blowfly pairing is combo-graph listed and unverified.
card_roles.Night's Whisper: Unconditional two-for-one at two mana. Life is a resource this deck spends freely.
card_roles.Obelisk Spider: Your best converter and the right tutor target once a source is online. It drains each opponent on counter *placement* rather than on death — several times faster than any death-trigger drain on a loop.
card_roles.Orcish Bowmasters: A flash body that pings on entry and on every extra opponent draw, amassing Orcs as it goes. A Game Changer, and rare instant-speed interaction in a list that has very little.
card_roles.Phyrexian Altar: A free outlet producing coloured mana — worth more than Ashnod's colourless in a BG deck with double-pip costs. Refuted as a Mikaeus infinite.
card_roles.Phyrexian Reclamation: Repeatable creature recursion at {1}{B} and 2 life — your answer to targeted removal on Yawgmoth or Mikaeus, and creature removal can't touch it.
card_roles.Pitiless Plunderer: Every other creature you control dying makes a Treasure — how the sacrifice half of the deck pays for itself. A combo-graph in-deck Skullclamp partner.
card_roles.Scurry Oak: A Squirrel whenever one or more +1/+1 counters land on it. Its Ivy Lane Denizen pairing is what the bracket engine called the deck's highest-bracket line, and stack 001 deliberately declined to rest the bracket floor on it — unverified.
card_roles.Sephiroth, Fabled SOLDIER // Sephiroth,: Sacrifice-for-a-card on entry and on attack, a drain on every other creature dying, and a transformation on the fourth resolution. The synergy graph lists it as an in-deck Hapatra partner at score 4 (Tokens + Sacrifice, -1/-1 + Death Trigger, Flying + Damage Trigger, Attack Trigger + Tokens).
card_roles.Serrated Arrows: Three counters across three turns from a colorless permanent — three Snakes and three shrinks, no coloured pips required.
card_roles.Skullclamp: The bodies-to-cards engine: every Snake, Insect, Faerie and Elf Warrior is a 1/1, so this is 'pay {1}, draw two' on repeat. Combo-graph in-deck partners include Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Mikaeus and Pitiless Plunderer.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colorless on turn one — what turns a turn-2 Hapatra into a turn-2 Hapatra plus a play.
card_roles.Survival of the Fittest: Repeatable creature filtering for {G} and a discard — barely a cost with Phyrexian Reclamation and Eternal Witness around. A Game Changer and the most powerful tutor in the list.
card_roles.Swiftfoot Boots: Hexproof and haste that still lets you target your own creature. On the Druid loop it nets only three green per cycle — the {1} equip comes due again every cycle once the Equipment falls off.
card_roles.The One Ring: Protection from everything for a turn when cast, then an escalating draw engine. A Game Changer whose burden counters are a real cost when you already pay life to Yawgmoth, Bitterblossom and three painlands.
card_roles.Toxic Deluge: The pure reset, and the sharp caveat: -X/-X until end of turn places no counters at all, so it triggers neither Hapatra nor Nest of Scarabs nor Necroskitter. Sequence it as the emergency button it is.
card_roles.Utility lands: Grim Backwoods and Lazotep Quarry give you sacrifice outlets and card draw off lands; Svogthos, the Restless Tomb is a late-game creature-land off a full graveyard; Opal Palace grows Hapatra past commander tax; Talon Gates of Madara phases out a creature on entry; The Mycosynth Gardens copies an artifact; Abstergo Entertainment is the deck's only graveyard-touching effect. One trap: Lazotep Quarry is the eighth mana-free outlet in the verified census, but {T} with no untapper means once per turn — it cannot loop.
card_roles.Vampiric Tutor: Any card to the top at instant speed for 2 life. A Game Changer that costs you a draw step — fire it on the turn the answer matters.
card_roles.Village Rites: One mana, sacrifice a creature, draw two at instant speed — the cheapest way to turn a Snake into cards in response to removal.
card_roles.Viscera Seer: A free outlet with library smoothing attached. Refuted as a Mikaeus infinite — one return, then the +1/+1 counter shuts it down.
card_roles.Walking Ballista: Removal that scales, and a verified kill piece with Mikaeus plus any free outlet. Mikaeus's anthem stops it from killing itself, so the third card is mandatory; without Mikaeus it's your best answer to a single problem creature.
card_roles.Worldly Tutor: Instant-speed creature to the top — Yawgmoth, Devoted Druid, Necroskitter or a converter. A Game Changer.
card_roles.Yahenni, Undying Partisan: A free sacrifice outlet on a hasty body that protects itself with indestructible. One of the six Mikaeus pairings stack 001 refuted — one undying return, not a loop.
card_roles.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: Your only free repeatable -1/-1 source, and therefore the tutor target that matters. The trap: a single instance of 'target' means an illegal target fizzles the whole ability — no counter, no draw — so a second body is mandatory, and the mandatory draw makes it library-bounded.
card_roles.Zulaport Cutthroat: A table-wide converter — each opponent loses 1 life per creature you control dying. This is the class that closes games; Blood Artist is not a substitute for it.

combo_lines.001:
The court takes up a seductive claim: that under Mikaeus, the Unhallowed, Hapatra's -1/-1 counter annihilates the +1/+1 counter undying leaves behind, restoring the creature as a legal undying target in perpetuity. Eight of the deck's nineteen listed two-card infinites rest on it. Four resolver passes and four adversarial checks later (checker verdict: pass), the holding is plain: the claim is FALSE as written — and the findings are worth more than the claim.

What survives, verified. **Mikaeus + Devoted Druid is a true two-card infinite** — of deaths, -1/-1 placements, Snakes and drain, and explicitly **not of mana**. The Druid's untap ability pays a -1/-1 counter as a cost, so it kills itself into a counterless graveyard and undying returns it cleanly. Now the clause everyone misreads: the returned Druid is a *new object* that has not been under your control since your turn began, so rule 302.6 forbids its {T} ability — three green on the first pass, **zero on every pass after**. The loop still runs forever, because the untap cost carries no tap or untap symbol and sits outside 302.6 entirely.

Steady state without haste: four counter placements, one death, zero mana per cycle. That is four Snakes a cycle with Hapatra out, one drain a cycle with Blood Artist, four drains a cycle with Obelisk Spider. Bolt on Lightning Greaves and the mana comes back — a **three-card, main-phase-only** line netting four green per cycle; Swiftfoot Boots nets only three, because the Equipment falls off the moment the Druid dies and the {1} equip is sorcery-speed, due again every single cycle. Greaves also hands the Druid shroud, locking Hapatra and Yawgmoth out of targeting it — know which you want before you fetch.

**Mikaeus + Walking Ballista is real, and it is a three-card line, not two.** Mikaeus's +1/+1 is a layer-7c modification applied alongside counters, so a Ballista with no counters left is a 1/1 under Mikaeus, not a 0/0 — it never dies on its own, the classic self-killing pattern is switched off, and an external free outlet is mandatory. With one, it is genuinely unbounded at 1 damage per iteration plus whatever the outlet yields, and it converts to a win with no drain payoff at all.

What is refuted. **Six of the listed infinites fail outright.** Mikaeus paired with Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Yahenni or Blasting Station yields exactly *one* undying return: the creature comes back wearing a +1/+1 counter, and on the second sacrifice the intervening 'if' is false — undying never triggers. Total output in the Altar case, four colorless and two drains; Carrion Feeder is actively anti-synergistic, since it *adds* +1/+1 counters. And the flagship misconception is worse still: **feeding Snake tokens to Mikaeus produces zero iterations** — state-based actions are performed first as a single event, a token in a zone other than the battlefield ceases to exist, and the Snake is gone before its undying trigger is even placed on the stack. Undying on a token is a dead grant; any line that reads 'sacrifice a Snake, get it back' is invalid on its face.

One finding worth the price of the whole scenario: **Yawgmoth loops for real, and it demands a second body.** His counter annihilates an undying +1/+1, so he clears the wall the six refuted outlets hit — but the ability contains a single instance of the word 'target', so if the creature you targeted is the creature you sacrificed, the whole ability fails to resolve and you do not even draw. Run it as an A/B loop across two non-Human creatures, or let Hapatra's Snakes fill the second slot. Each activation costs 1 life and the draw is mandatory: library-bounded — a strong engine, not a true infinite.

One trap to carry to the table. Counter annihilation *does* reset undying, but only when the annihilation and the death fall in **different** SBA checks. In the same check, last known information is read from before any of those actions — the +1/+1 counter is still visible and undying does not trigger. Strip the counter, let state-based actions run, then kill it separately.

Finally, what this scenario deliberately does **not** settle: eleven of the nineteen listed lines remain unresolved, and none may be spoken of as fact at your table or ours. The Blowfly Infestation family — Blowfly with Hapatra, with Nest of Scarabs, with Flourishing Defenses — is the deck's headline two-card kill, the one the goldfish tracks at 16.3% assembled and 12.5% by turn 6, and a scenario must settle whether the loop is optional enough to avoid a draw, whether it needs a seed counter and a spare token, and what happens when no legal target remains. **Needs a stack scenario.** Sharper still: Mikaeus gives other non-Human creatures +1/+1, and Snakes, Insects and Elf Warriors are all non-Human — if that anthem makes your own token fodder too big to die to your own -1/-1 counters, the deck's two flagship engines are mutually exclusive on the battlefield. **Needs a stack scenario, and it is the highest-value open question in the list.**

The Ivy Lane Denizen family is unresolved on both halves: Scurry Oak + Ivy Lane Denizen is the entry the bracket engine called the deck's highest-bracket line, and stack 001 pointedly refused to rest the floor on it, while the six outlet-paired Ivy Lane entries name outlets that cause nothing green to *enter* — the same projection artifact that inflated the Mikaeus count. **Needs a stack scenario.** So does Hapatra + Host of the Hereafter, elegant on oracle text and turning entirely on whether counter-*moving* counts as *putting*. The bracket floor of 4 holds regardless — on the 11 Game Changers plus the lines verified here. It simply does not hold on the number nineteen.

cover.identity: You are playing a converter, not a combo pile. Hapatra does not make -1/-1 counters at will — her first ability is a combat-damage trigger on an unevasive 2/2 — she monetises counters that *other* cards place, at a rate of one 1/1 deathtouch Snake per placement event. The 99 around her is built so that every counter becomes a body, every body becomes a card or a drain, and a narrow but genuine combo ceiling sits above a very strong grindy median.

how_it_wins:
Here's your first winning move: read Hapatra as a mint, not an engine. Her second ability pays out one 1/1 deathtouch Snake per placement *event* — other cards place the counters, she prints the bodies — so Black Sun's Zenith for three on one creature mints one Snake, while Black Sun's Zenith for one across six creatures mints six. Her combat trigger is never the plan: verified stack 001 (step 11) classifies it as a combat-damage trigger on an unevasive 2/2, worth at most one extra iteration per combat. She is, however, the most reliable card you own — turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 goldfish runs, mean 2.007, 99.9% by turn 6.

Because she's a mint, the scarce class is the *counter source*, and this is the trap most pilots never see. Stack 001's adversarial census counted eight sacrifice outlets that cost no mana — Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Yahenni, Yawgmoth, Blasting Station, and Lazotep Quarry once per turn — and exactly *one* of them, Yawgmoth, Thran Physician, also places a -1/-1 counter. The only other free repeatable source is Devoted Druid, and only while Mikaeus is out to reset it. Two cards deep — which is why your eight tutors are the engine room, not a luxury: one is drawn in 78.0% of games, 67.6% by turn 6.

The median game — most games — you win by out-carding three opponents and then draining them. Skullclamp turns every 1/1 into two cards for {1}; Grim Haruspex draws off each nontoken death; Deadly Dispute and Village Rites cash a spare body at instant speed; Morbid Opportunist collects once a turn no matter whose creatures die. And every deathtouch Snake blanks an attacker of any size, so the board that's drawing you cards is also the wall nobody wants to swing into. The goldfish names this game 'commander plus any -1/-1 payoff': 67.2% assembled, mean turn 3.62 — that's your real identity.

The ceiling is real, just narrower than the bracket sheet suggests — pilot it that way and you'll cash it more often, not less. The kill is a repeatable source feeding a converter that hits every seat: Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance or Obelisk Spider, with Blood Artist one tier down because he drains a single target player per death. Obelisk Spider is the tutor target worth naming — it drains on counter *placement* rather than death, roughly four times faster on any loop — and a drain converter is drawn in 51.9% of games, 41.5% by turn 6. Pivot when both halves are live and you've counted the table's spent interaction, and hold the honest line on the bracket: the floor of 4 stands on the 11 Game Changers, not on the inflated '19 two-card infinites' — knowing that keeps you dangerous.
mana_base:
For once, the audit gets to gloat. Twenty-four lands, and the tapped count is zero — not low, zero. Twenty-two are untapped duals, 22 of the 24 produce both colours, and black and green each count 23 land sources against a target of 22.

Lands alone put both colours at 91.8% on-curve. That clears the 90% yardstick before a single rock is counted, which almost never happens — in most builds the yardstick is what the ramp exists to rescue.

The pip ledger is lopsided and the base does not care. Black carries 71.4% of the pip load — 40.0 pips across 34 cards, up to triple-black in a single cost — against a 50% source share; green carries 28.6% against the same 50%. That disagreement is normally where an audit finds trouble; here it costs nothing, because when nearly every land makes both colours at once, the split cannot be wrong.

The producers push it further. Sixteen nonland sources — 9 rocks, 5 dorks, 2 rituals — lift on-curve to 97.2% black and 97.9% green, and tilt nonland sources green 10 to 8, because dorks are Forests with legs. Mind that Sol Ring, Mana Vault, Grim Monolith and Chrome Mox score zero coloured sources under the audit's unconditional-mana rule: they buy speed, not fixing. And that ramp is what makes 24 lands enough — the land-drop hit rate falls from 90.2% on turn 3 to 54.0% by turn 6, yet mean available mana still reads 6.15 that turn.

So what did the fleet's cleanest base actually pay? Life and a Spirit: City of Brass, Mana Confluence and Tarnished Citadel charge you to fix, and Forbidden Orchard hands an opponent a Spirit each tap — a Spirit that is, note, a legal target for your own -1/-1 counters. Restricted mana: none. The invoice for zero tapped lands is written on your life total and sixteen spell slots, and this deck was built to pay it.
matchups:
Sweeper control first, because you are built for it — and you will still sequence like you are not. Your token half is nearly free to lose. Bitterblossom rebuilds every upkeep for 1 life, and Skullclamp turns a 1/1 Snake into two cards for {1} — it gives +1/-1, so the Snake dies on equip. Grim Haruspex draws off every nontoken death, and Blood Artist triggers on ANY creature dying, so a table wrath with Blood Artist out is a large drain aimed wherever you like. That resilience was bought at deckbuild time — exactly what strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math means by buying resilience instead of restraint.

The asymmetry runs the other way on your combo half. Hapatra, Yawgmoth, Devoted Druid, Ivy Lane Denizen, Scurry Oak and Necroskitter are all creatures, so a wrath is close to one-sided against the half that wins and cheap against the half that grinds. Deploy in waves: tokens and cheap counter sources first, the enabler held in hand until the pivot window. Assume the wrath — over a four-player game one is near-certain.

Your own sweepers are not interchangeable, and this is the single most valuable sequencing fact in the matchup. Black Sun's Zenith puts X -1/-1 counters on each creature: it triggers Hapatra once per creature, feeds Nest of Scarabs, and hands Necroskitter every opposing creature that dies with a counter on it. That is a rebuild, not a reset. Toxic Deluge gives -X/-X until end of turn and places no counters — zero triggers for Hapatra, Nest and Necroskitter, with an additional cost of X life. It is a pure panic button; sequence it as one.

Heroic Intervention is the card that flips this matchup — hold it for the turn you go, not the turn you feel sad. One caution, stated plainly: on oracle text it grants hexproof and indestructible, which does not obviously answer a -X/-X effect that kills by toughness rather than destruction. That reading deserves its own stack scenario before you bet a game on it.

Against stax and tax the breadth gap gets its bill, and the honest coaching is that you cannot answer the archetype — you race it or you politick it. There is no artifact removal, no enchantment removal and no counterspell in the list, so a Sphere effect, a Winter Orb, a Blood Moon or a graveyard hoser sits there permanently. strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite names stax as "the hardest breadth test" and requires answers castable under the tax; you have none of the right class. Here is why I still like your seat — three reasons.

One: you are fast and cheap. 24 lands with zero entering tapped, 16 ramp producers — 9 rocks, 5 dorks and 2 rituals — including three zero-cost rocks, and a commander who lands on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 goldfish runs (mean 2.007). You are frequently under the lock before the second and third pieces layer — and layering is the whole game here, since strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial notes that one piece is an inconvenience while the compounding second and third are the lock.

Two: your engines are mana-free once assembled, which is the exact profile that survives a tax. Yawgmoth's activation costs 1 life and a body and no mana. The Devoted Druid loop's steady state produces four counter placements and one death per cycle at zero mana (verified stack 001 step 14), and Bitterblossom triggers on your upkeep for free. Recount your hand under the tax the way that section says — then notice the part of your deck that wins is the part the tax does not touch.

Three: you can tell the truth. strategy:multiplayer.politics warns that credibility is a multi-game resource, so say out loud that you are the seat with no artifact or enchantment answer, and ask the player holding the Krosan Grip to spend it. Keep the deal small, specific and expiring — one turn of your -1/-1 counters pointed elsewhere for one piece of enchantment removal.

And know your tutor default. Stack 001's final state names the target that matters: a free repeatable -1/-1 source, not any particular altar. A tutor is drawn in 78.0% of games, 67.6% by turn 6, mean turn 2.695 — under an assembling lock, fetch the source, then the converter, and take Green Sun's Zenith for Devoted Druid straight onto the battlefield when you need the tempo.

Against aggro you are favoured, and for a reason that never shows up in a removal count: a 1/1 deathtouch Snake is virtual interaction. It makes attacking into you a losing exchange regardless of the attacker's size, and a board of them turns an opposing creature deck's best cards into cards it cannot profitably use. That is strategy:card-advantage.virtual exactly — "a card that blanks several opposing cards generates advantage without drawing anything" — and the Commander correction is the part that matters: at a four-player table virtual advantage triples, because one effect can blank attack plans from three players at once, the cheapest way to answer roughly 120 life worth of aggression. Even trample trades up for you — you eat the overflow and their creature dies to a token that cost you nothing.

The goldfish puts mean bodies at 2.101 by turn 4 and 3.224 by turn 6, and that is a floor rather than a ceiling — the model simulates resource development rather than full games and counts bodies as creatures cast plus tokens parsed from "create ... token" text. Behind the Snakes, Black Sun's Zenith and Toxic Deluge are your catch-up buttons. Necroskitter converts their aggression into your board — it has wither, and any creature an opponent controls that dies with a -1/-1 counter on it comes back under your control.

One honesty flag: the frame's read that Necroskitter alongside Black Sun's Zenith is your single best card against a creature table is oracle reasoning only. Necroskitter is verified absent from the combo graph and the pairing has no stack scenario. Plan for it; do not promise it.

The real discipline here is life. This deck spends it constantly — Yawgmoth at 1 per activation, Phyrexian Reclamation at 2 per return, Bitterblossom every upkeep, The One Ring's burden counters, Toxic Deluge's additional cost, and City of Brass, Mana Confluence and Tarnished Citadel in the mana base — so your life total is a shared budget with your engine. Track which single opponent's clock is actually real and defend against that one rather than the table (strategy:multiplayer.pod-management). And do not convert a good matchup into a bad seat by attacking with Hapatra into open blockers for a marginal combat trigger.

Against combo you are thin in both directions — play it as a race, not an interaction game. You have no counterspell and no way to touch an artifact or enchantment kill, so the only combo decks you can interact with are creature-based. There you do hold real instant-speed answers: Grim Affliction, Fume Spitter's free sacrifice, Walking Ballista's counter-removal ping, Serrated Arrows' tap.

The answer-economy rule inverts in this matchup: held answers rot, and strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy says the last profitable moment against combo is now. Rank combo proximity above every board threat and re-rank every turn (strategy:threat-assessment).

Be honest about your own speed while you do it. 'Any drain converter' is drawn 51.9% of games, 41.5% by turn 6, mean turn 3.339. The Blowfly assembly is 16.3% overall, 12.5% by turn 6, mean turn 4.102 — and that line is unverified, one of eleven unresolved entries. You do not out-speed a dedicated combo deck on raw assembly, so do not plan to.

Plan instead to be the deck the table's interaction is not pointed at. Deploy Snakes that read as defensive, and take your window while three players watch each other (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection). Remember the tell: the moment a Mox, a Demonic Tutor or The One Ring hits the table, the cover the Snakes bought you is gone.

Against creature midrange you are in the seat this deck was built for, and you out-grind them on two axes at once: their removal is bad against tokens, and their attacks are bad into deathtouch. Hold single-target removal until a threat is pointed at you rather than spending it on sight — strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry is exact about why, since every one-for-one you cast spends a card, costs one opponent a card, and profits two bystanders for free.

The card that quietly dominates this matchup is Crumbling Ashes: an enchantment that destroys a creature with a -1/-1 counter on it at the beginning of each of your upkeeps. With any counter source that is a repeatable removal engine in a permanent class most fair creature decks cannot answer either. Seed with Fume Spitter or Grim Affliction and let Ashes do the rest. Every one of those placements is also a Snake.

The bodies-to-cards layer wins the long game: Skullclamp, Grim Haruspex, Morbid Opportunist, Deadly Dispute, Village Rites and Sephiroth turn a stream of 1/1s into a stream of cards. strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock names an engine that scales as a source of inevitability — four-player games trend long, so inevitability compounds and engines are the default winning plan.

Then pivot on a counted trigger, not a pretty board. Both halves live means a free repeatable -1/-1 source (Yawgmoth, or Mikaeus with Devoted Druid) plus a converter that hits every seat. Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance and Obelisk Spider each drain every opponent; Blood Artist drains one target player per death, which makes it a value card and a wrath tax rather than a table clock. Obelisk Spider is the fetch when the Druid loop is your kill: it drains on counter placement rather than on death, and stack 001 step 14 puts the no-haste steady state at four placements and one death per cycle — four drains per cycle instead of one.
mulligan:
The keep test is not 'does this hand have a payoff'. It's: **is there a route to a repeatable counter source?** Hapatra mints Snakes from counters other cards place, so a hand of Nest of Scarabs, Blood Artist and Zulaport Cutthroat with nothing placing counters is a hand of blanks waiting for a card you haven't drawn yet.

The numbers say you can afford to be picky and rarely have to be. The goldfish keeps its first seven 79.9% of the time (mean 0.243 mulligans), casts Hapatra on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 runs (mean 2.007, 99.9% by turn 6), and has a tutor in hand 67.6% of the time by turn 6. So a keep doesn't need to *contain* the engine — it needs lands, a turn-2 commander, and a card that finds one.

Keep on sight: two to four lands, Hapatra castable on turn 2, plus any of Yawgmoth, Devoted Druid, or any of the eight tutors. Keep two-landers with a dork or a mox — Birds of Paradise, Llanowar Elves, Elvish Mystic, Sol Ring, Lotus Petal, Dark Ritual — because that hand casts Hapatra on turn 1 or 2 with a play attached. Keep Skullclamp with any token maker; Bitterblossom alone is a card every other turn and rebuilds through wraths. And keep Blowfly Infestation as what it reliably is — a counter source — not as half of a two-card kill that has never been verified.

Ship these. Five or more lands with no tutor or dork: the curve's mean mana value is 2.19 and cannot use the seventh land. Drain converters (Blood Artist, Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance) with no source and no tutor — those are the blanks the mint metaphor warns about. Hands built around Mikaeus alone: he's your only six-drop, he's not a source by himself, and he's a combo piece for two specific partners, not a general-purpose enabler.

Ship one-landers even with a mox — a mox that finds no second land loses the commander. And treat hands whose only route is Scurry Oak, Ivy Lane Denizen or Host of the Hereafter as hands with *no* route: those lines are unresolved, and you don't mulligan-plan around a combo this manual won't assert.

On a mulligan to six, the priorities compress to exactly two things: lands that produce black on turn 2, and one card that either places counters repeatedly or finds one that does.
threat_assessment:
Start with the correction that reorganises everything else: Hapatra is a mint, not an engine. Her first ability is a combat-damage trigger on an unevasive 2/2 — stack 001 step 11 calls it "not an at-will repeatable placement," worth one extra iteration per combat at best. She does not make -1/-1 counters. She pays you a deathtouch Snake every time another card places them.

So the scarce resource is the counter SOURCE — not the outlet, not the payoff. Stack 001's census counted eight mana-free sacrifice outlets (Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Yahenni, Yawgmoth, Blasting Station, Lazotep Quarry) and exactly one, Yawgmoth, also places a counter. Everything downstream is abundant; the enabler class is two deep. Read your hands and your tutors through that lens — strategy:mulligans.engine-hands says payoffs without the enabler are blanks until the engine exists — and read the table through it too.

Now the hardest fact to own, and the one that drives your threat ranking from the pre-game onward: your interaction covers exactly one of the five permanent classes. Eight removal slots, two sweepers and four protection slots all answer creatures. There is no artifact removal, no enchantment removal, no counterspell and no land answer. The only graveyard-touching effect in the list is Abstergo Entertainment's {3}, {T}, exile-itself ability — it returns a historic card, exiles graveyards, and destroys nothing.

strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite is blunt about the cost: breadth before depth, because "three opponents mean every permanent type appears." So invert the usual habit. A creature is never the threat you fear most — you have eight answers, two sweepers and a wall of deathtouch for creatures. The threats that beat you are the ones you will never remove: a Sphere effect, Winter Orb, Blood Moon, a Rest-in-Peace-class hoser, a Rule-of-Law effect, an artifact or enchantment combo assembling in front of you.

strategy:threat-assessment says it straight: "an answer only counts when it matches a threat that actually beats you." Rank by permanent class before you rank by size. If two seats can present prison permanents, your role is decided before the first land drop — you do not own the long game under an assembling lock, so you are the beatdown racing the lock's completion (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial). Your outs are speed, politics and someone else's removal; name them out loud on turn one and sequence to protect them (strategy:resource-hedging.playing-to-outs).

Here is your asset: what the table sees early is cheap and defensive. Hapatra costs two and lands on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 goldfish runs (mean cast turn 2.007, median 2, 99.9% by turn 6), and 'commander plus any -1/-1 payoff' assembles 67.2% of the time at a mean turn of 3.623, 55.7% by turn 6. A 2/2 Cleric and a couple of 1/1 Snakes read as a defensive board — exactly the posture strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection tells you to buy.

But this list spends that cover faster than most, and the 11 Game Changers are the tell: Chrome Mox, Mox Diamond, Mana Vault, Grim Monolith, Demonic Tutor, Vampiric Tutor, Imperial Seal, Worldly Tutor, Survival of the Fittest, Orcish Bowmasters, The One Ring. The turn a Mox hits the battlefield or a Demonic Tutor resolves, the Snakes stop reading as chump blockers and start reading as a combo deck's early board. strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection notes the table discounts your "I haven't done anything" precisely because it tracks mana and draw engines.

So sequence like a politician. Lead with the token half and the cheap counter sources. Deploy fast mana on the turn it buys you a threat, not on turn one for its own sake, and fire tutors on a turn when someone else has just done something louder. The One Ring is the loudest card you own and it costs escalating life every upkeep — cast it when you want the cards, not when you want the protection turn to look clever.

The flip from ignored to archenemy has three concrete triggers, and all three are the second permanent — never Hapatra herself. First: Yawgmoth plus a second body with Hapatra out. Stack 001 step 12 verifies the shape — pay 1 life, sacrifice another creature, put a -1/-1 counter on up to one target creature and draw — and the trap inside it: the ability has a single instance of "target," so an illegal target on resolution means it does not resolve at all and you do not even draw. Hence the mandatory second body, and hence Hapatra's Snakes filling that slot.

The A/B loop repeats for real but is library-bounded by its own mandatory draw — a strong engine, not a true infinite. Any competent opponent kills Yawgmoth on sight. Do not present him into open mana unless the turn converts.

Second: Mikaeus, the Unhallowed alongside Devoted Druid — your one verified true two-card infinite (stack 001 steps 13-14). Infinite deaths, -1/-1 placements, Snakes and drain, and explicitly NOT mana: three green on the first pass and zero on every pass after, because the returned Druid is a new object and 302.6 blocks its tap ability. Steady state is four counter placements and one death per cycle at zero mana. With Blood Artist already on board it converts directly at one life per cycle from a player of your choice (step 16).

Third: Mikaeus plus Walking Ballista plus any free outlet — genuinely unbounded, and it converts to damage with no drain payoff at all. It is a three-card assembly, because Mikaeus's +1/+1 is a layer-7c modification that makes a counterless Ballista a 1/1 and switches off the classic self-kill (step 15). Mikaeus costs six; goldfish mean available mana is 6.150 on turn 6. 'Mikaeus + a free sacrifice outlet' is drawn 9.5% of the time overall, 5.8% by turn 6, mean turn 5.092 — and that target overstates its own value, because stack 001 refuted six of the eight Mikaeus entries it was built to track.

The last piece of threat management is aimed at your own self-image. The bracket-4 floor is safe — the 11 Game Changers carry it by themselves — but the '19 two-card infinites' figure in the bracket report is inflated, and you will not repeat it in a Rule 0 conversation or believe it at the table. Two lines are verified: Mikaeus + Devoted Druid, and Mikaeus + Walking Ballista as a three-card assembly.

Six are refuted outright by stack 001, checker verdict pass over four iterations. Mikaeus with Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Yahenni or Blasting Station each yields exactly one extra undying return. Snake tokens yield zero — a token in a zone other than the battlefield ceases to exist before its undying trigger is even placed on the stack.

Eleven remain unresolved: the three Blowfly Infestation entries, Scurry Oak + Ivy Lane Denizen, the six outlet-paired Ivy Lane entries, and Hapatra + Host of the Hereafter. None of the eleven may be spoken of as fact or tapped out for. The Blowfly line is the one the goldfish tracks (16.3% assembled, 12.5% by turn 6, mean turn 4.102), and it is exactly the one with no stack scenario behind it — treat it as a strong board, not a kill, until it is verified.

Separate ceiling from median and pace for the median (strategy:critical-mass, strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density). The median is genuinely strong — you out-card three opponents in most games without ever going off. And when you choose to be the archenemy, take one counted pivot window rather than the first loop that looks live: strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window says assume every held answer appears the moment you present lethal. Count the table's open mana first, and prefer the attempt that leaves Bitterblossom, Snakes and a drain converter behind if it fails.
upgrades:
Ten names render below, and the arithmetic behind them comes first: this deck carries no sideboard, so all ten are pool scouts — a first read over 11,831 eligible cards, ranked by what each adds to the engines stack 001 verified. Zero arrive from a bench; every one earned its slot against the whole pool. The top half extends the Yawgmoth loop and the Snake-minting converter directly — Ayara, First of Locthwain and Warren Soultrader lead — and each scout arrives with a tagged combo line that rides machinery you already sleeve.

Read the evidence tiers before you fall in love. Every combo line a scout opens carries the same stamp — needs a stack scenario — because stack 001's census cut both ways: it verified the Druid loop and refuted six outlet pairings that looked just as good on paper, and a scout's tagged line meets that bar or stays a projection. Note, too, what the numbers refuse to move: bracket 4 before, bracket 4 after, on every entry. These are engine extensions, not power-level escalations.

The famous names that miss the list lose on a read of the card, not on reputation. The Great Henge (rank 235) prices off greatest power, and a board of 1/1 Snakes leaves it near nine mana; Gravecrawler's graveyard clause needs a Zombie, and the deck controls exactly one (Host of the Hereafter); Triskelion adds little that in-deck Walking Ballista doesn't already do — stack 001 step 15 shows the same Mikaeus line as a three-card assembly with any of the deck's eight free outlets. The ten below are what beat them.
